topic: The Building Blocks of Space: Span, Dependence, and Bases
target_audience: University students beginning Linear Algebra or advanced STEM high school students

outline.topic: The Building Blocks of Space: Span, Dependence, and Bases
outline.target_audience: University students beginning Linear Algebra or advanced STEM high school students

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Vector-Bot’s Movement
sections.content: Introduce the fundamental operations: Scaling (multiplying a vector by a number) and Addition (tip-to-tail). Establish the visual metaphor of a robot named 'Vector-Bot' that can only move in directions provided by specific arrows.
sections.example: Vector-Bot has two arrows: $\vec{v}$ (1 unit right) and $\vec{w}$ (1 unit up). To reach position (2,3), the robot must scale $\vec{v}$ by 2 and $\vec{w}$ by 3, then add them together.

sections.title: Linear Combinations: The Recipe
sections.content: Define a linear combination as the sum of scaled vectors: $a\vec{v} + b\vec{w}$. Use a graphical 'grid-warping' animation to show how changing scalars $a$ and $b$ moves the robot to different coordinates.
sections.example: If $\vec{v} = [1, 0]$ and $\vec{w} = [0, 1]$, then $3\vec{v} + (-2)\vec{w}$ is a linear combination resulting in the vector $[3, -2]$.

sections.title: The Span: Reachable Territory
sections.content: Define 'Span' as the set of all possible linear combinations of a group of vectors. Visualize this as 'painting' the space. One vector spans a line; two non-collinear vectors span a flat plane.
sections.example: Imagine Vector-Bot has two vectors pointing in the same direction. He is stuck on a single line. But if they point in different directions, he can 'paint' (span) the entire 2D floor.

sections.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Arrow
sections.content: Introduce Linear Dependence. If one vector can be created by a linear combination of others, it is 'dependent' and adds no new 'reach' to the span. Graphically, show a third vector falling onto the plane already created by two others.
sections.example: Vector-Bot has $\vec{v}=(1,0)$, $\vec{w}=(0,1)$, and a third 'helper' $\vec{u}=(1,1)$. Since $\vec{u} = \vec{v} + \vec{w}$, the third vector is redundant (linearly dependent). It doesn't help the robot reach any new heights.

sections.title: Bases: The Minimalist Toolkit
sections.content: Define a 'Basis' as a set of vectors that are: 1) Linearly Independent (no redundancy) and 2) Span the entire space. It is the 'optimal' set of directions to describe a coordinate system. Highlight that there can be many different bases for the same space.
sections.example: For a 2D map, a Basis is like having exactly two non-parallel arrows. If you have only one, you can't reach the whole map. If you have three, one is a 'copycat.' Two unique arrows are the 'Basis' for your 2D world.

storyboard.title: Prerequisites: The Vector-Bot’s Movement
lecture_lines: Meet Vector-Bot, our guide to the linear world.
He moves by scaling and adding his arrow tools.
Scale a vector to change its length and direction.
animations: A small robot icon appears at (0,0) on a grid to represent Vector-Bot.
A red arrow v from (0,0) to (1,0) stretches to (2,0) with label '2v' in #FF0000.
A blue arrow w appears at (0,0) to (0,1), then its tail moves to the tip of 2v at (2,0) in #0000FF.
A purple vector u appears from (0,0) to (2,1) and is labeled '2v + w' in #800080.
The coordinates (2,1) flash in yellow #FFFF00 next to the robot at its final position.

storyboard.title: Linear Combinations: The Recipe
lecture_lines: A linear combination scales and adds multiple vectors together.
Vector-Bot uses these "recipes" to reach new coordinates.
Watch how changing the scalars moves him across space.
Scale vector v by a and vector w by b.
Their sum a*v + b*w determines his final destination.
animations: The formula a*v + b*w appears in the center in white #FFFFFF.
A coordinate grid appears; a dot representing the combination moves as a and b scalars vary.
Red vector v scales to 3 units right, blue w scales to 2 units down; resultant points to (3,-2).

storyboard.title: The Span: Reachable Territory
lecture_lines: The Span is every point Vector-Bot can possibly reach.
One vector spans a single line of infinite points.
Two non-parallel vectors can "paint" an entire 2D plane.
Think of Span as the full territory covered.
If vectors align, the Span collapses to a line.
animations: The word 'SPAN' appears in bold yellow #FFFF00 in the center.
A single vector v appears; a faint grey line #808080 extends infinitely through it.
A second vector w is added; the 2D plane begins to be 'painted' with light blue #ADD8E6.
The vector w rotates to align with v; the painted plane area shrinks back into a line.
The 2D plane is fully filled with color #ADD8E6 to represent the full span of two independent vectors.

storyboard.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Arrow
lecture_lines: Linear dependence means one vector is actually redundant.
It can be built using the other available arrows.
Adding a dependent vector doesn't expand the reachable Span.
The third vector falls onto the existing 2D plane.
It adds "backup" but no new directions for movement.
animations: Show vectors v(1,0) and w(0,1) in #FFFFFF, then add vector u(1,1) in red #FF0000.
Vectors v and w move tip-to-tail to reach the tip of u; u flashes red #FF0000 to show redundancy.
The word 'DEPENDENT' appears in red #FF0000 above the redundant vector u.

storyboard.title: Bases: The Minimalist Toolkit
lecture_lines: A Basis is a minimal set of independent directions.
It must span the space without any redundant arrows.
Many different bases can describe the same 2D world.
animations: The words 'Linearly Independent' and 'Spans Space' appear in green #00FF00.
Two arrows i and j appear at right angles in #00FF00 to form a basis.
Remove arrow j; the painted span area on the grid shrinks from a plane to a single line.
Show i, j, and a diagonal vector; the diagonal vector turns grey #808080 to indicate it is extra.
Highlight the two independent vectors i and j in #00FF00 and label them 'Basis'.
